en: Blocked the way from the hills.
Kojozhash surpassed all in marksmanship;
A hulking mountain upon the ridge,
He hid among the feather grass,
Dressed in bright red colors,
Running ahead of an arrow,
The wind could not match his trot,
No beast could match his stride.
(The Chinese fled from ridge to ridge,
Rushed away.)
While Chubak wielded his sword,
Then Kojozhash, Karazhoy's son,
Clad in green, changing his appearance,
Chubak before him,
Oh hero, lay watching him.
Then grease came from his thumb;
Of that enraged infidel,
Blood came from his nails.
Without staggering or hurrying in confusion,
Never missing the point he fixed his gaze on,
The dog's trigger stood ready;
A master in marksmanship.
Chubak, Akbaltay's son,
Oh hero, his appointed death had come!
From a whip's length to his flank,
With a steel bullet in his hand,
Then the practiced marksman fired once!
Oh hero, the matchlock shot struck his belly,
Fire flashed upon Chubak's breast!
Then, with life barely remaining,
Amid dust that hid the earth,
The yellow gold taken from Beijing,
He scattered it as he went—did you see?
Your Chubak, turned coward, toward his people,
Fled away—did you see?
Was a young wife of seventeen,
Chubak, Khan Baltay's son,
Fled away to his people.
Down the single road of It-Ölbös,
He fled and escaped.
Kögala, the supernaturally supported racer,
Akbaltay's only son,
Oh hero, carried him away in flight and escaped.
The handful of the Islamic faith,
Turned back and rushed away.
The swine dressed in green, changing his appearance;
Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Hero Shygay of the Zhediger,
He struck both together with one shot.
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
Zhamgyrchy of the Eshtek—
Bokmurun and hero Shygay,
When those two fell to bullets,
The seven khans remaining,
All gathering their courage,
Old Koshoy among them,
Fell upon Kojozhash.
Falling upon Kojozhash,
When they fought in tumult,
Kojozhash, Karazhoy's son,
Could not be caught by the eye.
That exceptional dog, master of every trick,
His whereabouts could not be known.
Escaping up into the hills,
At the swarming Buruts,
He loosed arrows like rain.
That formidable, practiced dog
Fired bullets like hail.
The painted short gun with steel bullets,
Adding its report to report,
He fired a thousand times with it;
Before its bullets reached them,
The painted arrow in his hand,
With it he shot a hundred times.
The white arrow with a ravenous mouth,
With it he shot fifty times.
The painted short gun beneath him,
With it he shot forty times.
When his countless bullets struck,
Then Serek, the leopard hero, died;
A wolf like the diviner died;
Blue-maned heroes died, a multitude died.
Akayar, who lifted camels,
Their champions died as well.
Akzholtoy, Archa Khan's son,
Struck by a bullet, he died too,
To the four corners of the world,
He used to carry full and faithful news;
Lord Shuutu died as well.
Akzholtoy, who could snap a rope,
The young man close to Manas, died;
Baychoro, Baabedin Khan's son,
Then young Baychoro died as well.
Then your renowned Alma alone,
Turning back into Beijing,
Your Alake was left alone,
Parted from his champions.
His many sorrows would not fit in his breast;
Your blue-maned hero Alma, alone,
His tears streamed in ten channels!
Clashing in fury,
Against the countless black Kalmyks before him,
Standing his ground and fighting,
Shouting, “Sovereign!”
Crying the battle cry, “Manas!”
At the black infidels before him,
Your Alake kept driving and scattering them.
Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
Your Alake made the Chinese bellow,
Kept hemming them in and driving them.
Beyond the desert of It-Ölbös,
Your Khan Alma drove them across,
Drove them onward.
Shouting now and then,
The infidels like black willows,
He drove back and scattered.
Behind him, the forty companions
Had become his support.
Upon the plundered Chinese,
Your Alake avenged Chubak.
When he reached the rough sands,
He slaughtered those on gray horses;
When he entered the mountain cleft,
Their khan fell into his hands;
Then he slaughtered those on black horses.
Your Alake sped upon Sarala;
The khans who faced him,
Almambet struck in the waist,
Then flung them like feedbags.
Through their center, your lion Alma
Was boring his way;
Then upon one flank, Khan Töshtük
Was slaughtering them.
Their very center, the forty champions
Had surrounded.
The Muslims gathered their horses,
Were plundering them.
The gullies filled with bodies face down,
Were filled to the brim.
Taking red gold and jewels,
Those who survived the dead,
Good heavens, were prospering.
When your noble Alma entered,
When he struck toward Beijing,
The many Chinese, the countless Manchus,
Distraught and staggering,
Were thrown into panic.
Their cruppers snapped,
Their saddles slipped onto their horses' necks;
Oh hero, still more rushed about.
Their saddle-girths snapped;
Unable to gather their wits, panting,
Still more were fleeing.
Of the Chinese with red tassels,
This was where their mighty ones were slaughtered;
Of the Chinese with rank buttons,
This was where so many were slaughtered.
Then their khans, Jangjung foremost, died;
The infidels' hero Kara, the champion, died as well.
Kongurbay remained alone.
Suffering and shouting,
The swine was in a sorry state.
Algara's head,
Kongurbay kept turning.
Then his club-like forelock,
Shouting beyond restraint,
Kongurbay kept tearing out.
A wretch skilled among spearmen,
A formidable wretch who knew the enemy's tricks,
He raged and struggled,
Then pleaded with Kojozhash:
“Why should I speak of the others?
Hero, a fire burning in meadow grass is dreadful;
Worse still, an enemy from one's own people.
A confidant is dangerous; a secret is dangerous.
He learned your secrets and left;
That champion of yours, the dog Alma, is dreadful!
Again he meant to rob me of sleep,
Again he raided my horses on the Irtysh;
For six months Beijing was blood,
He scattered my wealth like charcoal.
He slaughtered so many of my people,
My support in whom I trusted;
That fugitive burned
My well-defended land.
He killed all the sentries;
His renowned lord Manas,
He thus made khan of Beijing.
I had fed him my salt so often,
He plundered and carried off my daughter.
He robbed me of sleep.
At first we were the people of forty khans;
Hero, he slaughtered my people.
Consent to what I say, hero;
Why should I speak of the others?
Just shoot Almambet for me!
If you shoot Almambet dead,
The worthy khan, Sultan Manas,
Oh hero, we shall capture alive.
To the eighty girls in Beijing,
Hero, we shall take him and put him to stud.
Then, if a boy is born,
Over Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
We shall raise him as khan!”
Before the grim-faced one could finish his plan,
Almambet, who had been watching,
His sword ringing in his hand,
His battle-axe chiming at his waist,
His painted spear sweeping in his hand,
Then, with his waist bound tight,
Looking like dusk and mist,
Taking the form of a night death-spirit,
Then rumbling and gathering speed,
Had reached them.
With the aspect of a hungry lion,
If you looked at him from the front,
He had the dread presence of six thousand warriors;
If you looked at him from behind,
He had the form of a dragon.
Readying his keen steel,
Venom pouring from his mouth,
He rose towering over the ridge,
Looking like a dragon.
When he saw Almambet's appearance,
The grim-faced wretch began to think:
“Sarala beneath him,
No beast can match him in a race;
Against this raging fugitive,
No strength can suffice in battle.
Let me merely pretend to flee;
Let me plunge him into deep misery.
If he falls alive into my hands,
Let me take boundless vengeance on the dog.
Torturing him once every seven steps,
Let me thus cast him into fire!”
Then Almambet came out upon the ridge,
Fired once with his painted gun;
Unable to withstand his fury,
The Manchus fled with a rush.
Over a saddle-shaped ridge,
Kongurbay passed.
Algara beneath him,
He whipped on either side;
Kongurbay fled.
“God, deliver the Manchu to me!” he said.
Without looking around,
Almambet pursued in earnest,
Not sparing his life at all.
Your Alma struggled, unable to catch him,
Pleading with Sarala:
“Today, my companion in suffering, Sarala,
Lower your head to the ground;
Take strides like a wild sheep.”
Sarala beneath him,
Your Alake struck Sarala on the thigh;
Then a long trail of dust stretched out.
